nameStory: The ebony spleenwort gets its name from its striking dark, reddish-brown stem that's as glossy as polished ebony wood. Like other spleenworts, it was historically believed to cure disorders of the spleen, though we now know this medieval belief was based on the fern's kidney-shaped spore clusters rather than any actual medicinal properties. The lustrous dark stem creates a beautiful contrast against the bright green fronds.
description: Ebony spleenwort is a small, elegant fern that grows in neat clusters from rocky crevices and ledges. It produces two different types of fronds: tall, upright fertile fronds that reach 8-20 inches and release spores, and shorter sterile fronds that stay green all winter and lie close to the ground. The most striking feature is the glossy, dark reddish-brown stem that runs up the center of each frond, supporting neat rows of small, pointed leaflets. This hardy little fern is evergreen, providing greenery even in the depths of winter.

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: The stem (stipe) and midrib are dark reddish-brown to nearly black with a glossy, almost varnished appearance that feels smooth to the touch - like polished wood

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Two types of fronds: tall upright fertile ones that die back in winter, and shorter evergreen sterile ones that lie flat and persist through cold weather

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Small leaflets (pinnae) alternate along the stem rather than growing directly opposite each other, and each has a small ear-like projection (auricle) pointing toward the frond tip

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spore clusters appear as short brown lines along the underside of fertile fronds, covered by narrow flaps that split open when mature

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Grows from rock crevices, stone walls, and cliff faces, often seeming to sprout directly from solid stone with little visible soil

habitat: Look for ebony spleenwort growing from cracks in rocks, old stone walls, cliff faces, and rocky outcrops throughout New England's hills and mountains. It thrives in well-drained, often alkaline soil that collects in rock crevices, and can tolerate both partial shade and fairly sunny exposures. You'll often find it alongside other rock-loving plants like wild columbine and rock polypody fern.

seasonality.spring: New fiddleheads emerge from the base of the plant, unfurling into fresh green fronds while the old evergreen sterile fronds remain from the previous year.
seasonality.summer: Both fertile and sterile fronds are fully developed, with the tall fertile fronds standing upright and the shorter sterile ones spreading close to the ground.
seasonality.fall: Spores mature and are released from the brown sori on the undersides of fertile fronds, which begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Only the evergreen sterile fronds persist, lying close to rocks and remaining green even under snow cover.

funFact: This clever fern can clone itself by growing tiny plantlets near the base of its stems - when soil covers these buds, they develop into entirely new ferns as the parent frond dies, essentially allowing the plant to 'walk' to new locations over time.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with maidenhair spleenwort, which also has a dark stem but has opposite (not alternate) leaflets and smaller, more delicate fronds. Remember: ebony spleenwort's leaflets alternate like stairs, while maidenhair spleenwort's leaflets face each other like mirror images.
contextualKnowledge: This species has had a confusing taxonomic history - it was long called Asplenium ebeneum in many older field guides, so you might see both scientific names used for the same plant. The name 'spleenwort' comes from medieval herbalists who thought the kidney-shaped spore clusters indicated the plant could cure spleen ailments, following the old 'doctrine of signatures' belief that plants resembled the body parts they could heal.
compareHints: Among New England spleenworts, ebony spleenwort is distinguished by its alternating (not opposite) leaflets and two different frond types. Maidenhair spleenwort has opposite leaflets and more delicate fronds, while walking fern has long, undivided fronds that taper to rooting tips. Mountain spleenwort has bluish-green fronds and grows only on acidic rocks, unlike ebony spleenwort which prefers limestone and other alkaline rocks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spleenworts, maidenhair spleenwort is the smallest and most rock-loving species.

Walking fern is completely unique among New England spleenworts with its simple, undivided fronds - all other local Asplenium species like maidenhair spleenwort and ebony spleenwort have typically ferny, divided fronds.
Wall-rue is much smaller than its spleenwort relatives and is the only one that grows exclusively on limestone rocks.
Among New England spleenworts, mountain spleenwort is unique for its extremely fine, lacy frond divisions and blue-green color.
Green spleenwort is the only New England spleenwort with consistently green stems and midribs.
